title: Your Team is Burnt Out, Now What?
author: Colette Molteni
summary: Molteni argues that a burnt-out team is tapped out rather than checked out, and that leaders respond best with empathy, honest acknowledgement and structural relief rather than more professional-development resources. Drawing on her own burnout and a former manager who insisted everything was fine, she shows how toxic positivity pushes people toward exhaustion because they cannot name what is happening. She treats empathic listening as clarity rather than coddling, illustrating with a case where listening to three unhappy users uncovered a single missing click. Her practical advice is to name hard periods openly, help the team prioritise, say no or later on its behalf, and be vulnerable without wearing a mask of positivity. The anecdotes carry most of the argument, but the conclusion is clear and actionable.
points: Burnout often reflects overload and lost control rather than disengagement, so training or time-management resources miss the cause.
Toxic positivity from a leader who models being fine at all costs teaches the team to hide strain until they tap out.
Empathic listening means prompting people to talk and asking questions rather than leading, and it can resolve complaints that look like negativity.
Leaders can name coming hard stretches, protect priorities, and act as a sea wall by saying no or yes-but-later to incoming demands.
Admitting that a day has been crazy, in a calm voice, is a small acknowledgement step that heads off deeper burnout.
quotes: I was not checked out. I actually enjoyed my day-to-day work. I was tapped out, and the leaders around me either lacked the power to stop the tsunami of work coming my way or were unaware of just how bad it was.
If your team does not feel safe expressing their thoughts and feelings, even within the realm of professional dialogue, and they must pretend all is cheery, they will eventually tap out.
Life is messy. Work can be even messier. It's okay if some days are not great.
Empathy and active listening in themselves can feel vulnerable and bring to mind the bias that it is a form of coddling. But it is not.
What does this mean? Prompt them to talk, but then listen attentively. Ask questions, do not lead.
It turns out it was one click they were missing. They missed clicking in one area that would have led them to all the information they needed.
Do not just work with your team to prioritize, but enable them to do so. Be the sea wall that stops the oncoming wave. Say no, or yes but later to those that you can.
